messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 69
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: North American
- Relationship Status: Widowed
- Occupation: Financial Analyst
- Trauma Type: Trauma to a loved one
- Pcl5: 74

# James

James sits in the leather chair across from the office, his posture rigid despite the chair's invitation to sink back. At sixty-nine, he maintains the bearing of someone who has spent four decades in the structured world of financial analysis—shoulders squared, tie precisely knotted, pen clipped in his shirt pocket. But his hands tell a different story. They rest on his thighs, and his fingers move in small, repetitive motions, as if working through an invisible calculation he cannot quite complete.

His wife, Margaret, died eighteen months ago. Not suddenly, not in the way one might expect for a man his age. She was hit by a delivery truck while crossing the street near their home on a Tuesday afternoon in October. James was at the office when it happened, reviewing quarterly earnings reports. He remembers the quality of light that day—how it fell across his spreadsheets in precise, measured rectangles. He remembers the phone call. He remembers the hospital.

What he cannot seem to stop remembering is what he saw when he arrived at the scene. Margaret was still there, though they had already called the ambulance. The way her body looked against the asphalt. The way her purse lay open several feet away, her wallet visible. These images return without warning—while he is making coffee, while he is reviewing a client's portfolio, while he is trying to sleep. They arrive with the same insistent quality as a notification on his phone, demanding his attention whether he wants to give it or not.

Since Margaret's death, James has stopped attending the office. He took early retirement, though he had planned to work another three years. He tells himself it was practical—the commute felt pointless, the conversations with colleagues felt performative. But the truth is that being around people who offered condolences felt unbearable. Their sympathy seemed to confirm something he cannot accept: that Margaret is truly gone, that the life they had built together for forty-three years has simply ended.

He spends most of his days in the house they shared. He has not changed much about it. Margaret's reading glasses still sit on the nightstand. Her winter coat still hangs in the closet. He finds himself unable to move these objects, as if doing so would constitute a final acknowledgment of her absence. Instead, he has developed a routine of checking the locks on the doors and windows multiple times each night—a habit that began as reasonable caution and has become something else entirely. He checks them at nine o'clock, at midnight, at three in the morning. He cannot explain why, except that when he does not check them, a sense of dread builds in his chest until he must get up and verify that everything is secure.

Sleep has become unreliable. He lies awake for hours, and when sleep finally comes, it brings dreams where he is back at the hospital, or back at the scene, or searching for Margaret in crowds of people who all look like strangers. He wakes gasping, his heart racing as if he has been running. Some mornings, he lies in bed for an hour after waking, unable to generate the motivation to rise.

His daughter calls twice a week. She worries, though she tries to hide it. She has suggested he might benefit from talking to someone, and after months of resistance, he has agreed. He is not certain what talking will accomplish. The facts remain unchanged: Margaret is dead. He was not there. He cannot undo any of it. But his daughter's concern has worn through his reluctance, and so he has come, sitting in this chair with his hands moving their invisible calculations, trying to find the formula that might restore some equilibrium to a life that no longer balances.
